title: Permutation Group
body:
A [[Group]] whose elements are **bijections of a set to itself**, with composition as the
operation. The identity is the do-nothing map, inverses exist because bijections are invertible,
and composition is associative because function composition always is. So the axioms come free;
the only thing to check for a particular collection is closure.

> **Homograph warning.** [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) uses *permutation* for a **count**:
> $P(n,r) = n!/(n-r)!$, how many ordered arrangements exist. This course uses it for an
> **object**: one particular rearrangement, viewed as a function. The two meet at $n!$, which is
> both the answer to "how many orderings of $n$ things" and the order of the [[Symmetric Group]]
> $S_n$. See [[Permutation]] for the counting sense.

## Cycle notation

Writing a permutation as a table of inputs and outputs is unreadable. Chase each element instead
and record the loops:

```
      1 2 3 4 5
σ =   3 5 1 4 2      as a table

σ = (1 3)(2 5)       as cycles;  4 is fixed and omitted
    read: 1→3, 3→1, 2→5, 5→2
```

Every permutation factors into **disjoint** cycles, uniquely up to order, and disjoint cycles
commute. Two facts fall straight out:

- **The order of $\sigma$ is the lcm of its cycle lengths.** A $(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$ has order 6:
  the 3-cycle returns every 3 steps, the transposition every 2, and everything is home together
  at 6. See [[GCD and LCM]].
- **Composition is right-to-left**, like function composition, and it is not commutative:
  $(1\,2)(1\,3) \ne (1\,3)(1\,2)$. Non-abelian groups start here.

## Transpositions and parity

A **transposition** is a 2-cycle, a single swap. Every permutation is a product of
transpositions, in many ways: $(1\,2\,3) = (1\,3)(1\,2)$, and you could pad that with any
cancelling pair. What is **not** free to vary is the parity of how many you used.

**The parity of a permutation is well defined.** Every decomposition of a given $\sigma$ into
transpositions has the same parity, so "even" and "odd" are properties of $\sigma$ itself. A
$k$-cycle is a product of $k-1$ transpositions, so it is even exactly when $k$ is odd, which is
the off-by-one everyone gets wrong once.

Parity is what [[Alternating Group]] is built from, and it is the same invariant that makes the
sign of a [[Determinant]] work: the $\pm$ in the permutation expansion of $\det$ is exactly the
parity of the permutation being summed over. That is not an analogy, it is the same function.

## Why they are the general case

**Cayley's theorem: every group is isomorphic to a permutation group.** Given $G$, send each $g$
to the map $x \mapsto gx$. That map is a bijection of $G$ (cancellation gives injectivity), and
the assignment respects the operation, so $G$ embeds in the symmetric group on its own elements.
See [[Isomorphism]] and [[Homomorphism]].

The consequence is that studying permutation groups is not studying a special case. It is
studying all finite groups with a concrete handle attached, which is why the course spends the
whole of the group block here.

## The three named families

| Group | Elements | Order |
|---|---|---|
| [[Symmetric Group]] $S_n$ | all permutations of $n$ symbols | $n!$ |
| [[Alternating Group]] $A_n$ | the even ones | $n!/2$ |
| [[Dihedral Group]] $D_n$ | symmetries of a regular $n$-gon, as permutations of its vertices | $2n$ |
